definition: Auspicious means favorable; suggesting that success is likely to come — a promising sign, not present-tense joy.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word auspicious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know auspicious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The bakery's first morning felt auspicious: a line out the door before the ovens had even finished heating.
Encouraging signs merely lift your hopes; auspicious signs point clearly toward a successful outcome ahead.
Providential is stronger than auspicious — good fortune so perfectly timed it seems arranged by fate itself.

Promising means showing signs of future success, and it usually attaches to the thing with potential itself -- a promising student, a promising script. Auspicious attaches instead to the signs and circumstances around a beginning: the timing, the omens, the early turnout. The violinist is promising; her opening night is auspicious.

Favorable means working in your favor right now -- favorable terms, a favorable review, a favorable ruling all give you a present advantage. Auspicious is future-facing: it reads early signs as pointing toward success still to come. A favorable ruling helps you today; an auspicious start only predicts good things ahead.

The last frost came two weeks early, the hardware store donated a truckload of topsoil unasked, and forty families signed up for twenty plots.

Nothing has actually succeeded yet — the word fits because the early frost date, free topsoil, and long waitlist are all signs pointing toward future success.

Then, the week of the debut, everything turned.
The hall's error meant a bigger room.
On the night itself, the signs felt auspicious to everyone backstage: a sold-out house, three local critics in the seats, and a donor asking about next season before the downbeat.
